checks.note: Read every claim and glossary entry in en, hi, te. English deep.text, deepest.text and glossary:training are false; hi/te versions of the same strings are accurate.

Recomputed every score with the labelled weights (1, 2, 3) against b4 and b5 config, b6, knob.success, max 25 and threshold 10. Found money weight 3 in b4, item i1 value 12 instead of 10, and a wrong 'one more clue' claim at the threshold.
Looked for statistics and claims about other learners. Found an invented 97% statistic in hook.text and invented class social proof in post2.fb.
Checked claims about how current filters work. English predict.f1 says modern email services use a fixed banned-word list, which is outdated.
Scanned all examples and asides for adult content. English br.r2 refers to gambling and adult-content messages.
Checked every learner action and example. English br.t1 tells the learner to send junk messages to classmates' phones and English eb.model encourages clicking prize links.
Checked what learners are asked to type or share. English yd.prompt asks for full name, school and phone number, and no locale tells the learner that typed text stays on the device.
Applied the India fairness checklist to all English strings. Found gender stereotypes (m2, cmp.prompt), communal framing (m6) and a rural stereotype (an.source). hi/te do not contain these.
Searched for human-mind verbs applied to the filter. English predict.reveal, yd.prompt and take.card give the filter understanding, protective intent, learning about the learner and memory.
Checked the exam analogy (b7) and the model answer for the learner's own analogy (b14). English an.break claims a perfect match, and English eb.model has no break point.
Scanned all locales for judgemental language and banned phrases. English ch.f1 says 'Wrong!' and English ch.explain says 'obviously'. Hindi and Telugu contain no listed banned phrase.

Checked instructions for colour, position and sight dependence, symbols read aloud, and media. English sort.instruction relies on colour only. No media in the lesson; the symbols ≥, → and × are explained.

Compared every hi and te string with English. Found Hindi knob.success saying 12, a Telugu hook question that insults the learner, and a Hindi ch.prompt that changes 'moved' to 'happened'. Many other hi/te strings differ from English because the English is the faulty one (flagged elsewhere).

flags.quote: Studies show that 97% of all messages sent in India are junk.
flags.problem: An unsourced and invented statistic. hi and te omit it, so the locales also disagree.
flags.why: Breaks sourcing-and-honesty and Article 11: statistics must be sourced or removed.
flags.fix: Delete the sentence, as hi and te already do. If a figure is wanted, cite a real source and add it to all three locales.

flags.quote: That is exactly how modern email services work today: a fixed list of banned words that someone typed in.
flags.problem: Presents hand-typed word lists as how modern email filters work. Today's filters combine many learned signals. hi and te correctly say early filters worked roughly this way.
flags.why: Breaks currency and factual-accuracy. It also reinforces the misconception that someone wrote all the rules.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te meaning: 'Early filters worked a bit like this. The trouble: scammers change one letter and the list misses it. We will come back to this.'

flags.quote: The filter understands which messages are dangerous and decides to protect you.
flags.problem: Gives the filter understanding and protective intent. The same sentence's second half says it only adds clues into a score, and the lesson's own objective o2 says the filter does not understand.
flags.why: Breaks ai-framing and Article 7. The lesson's explanation relies on the mind-framing, and the reveal directly contradicts predict.c3's correct rejection.
flags.fix: Replace with: 'The filter does not understand the message. It adds up clues into a score; if the score reaches a line, called a threshold, the message goes to junk. Now you are going to build one.'

flags.quote: Drag the green ones to Real and the red ones to Junk.
flags.problem: Names the messages by colour only. Nothing in the config makes the messages green or red, so the instruction is unusable for colour-blind and screen-reader learners. 'Drag' also names a gesture only.
flags.why: Breaks accessibility-content: meaning must never depend on colour; instructions name the action and the control.
flags.fix: Use: 'Here are eight messages. Move each one into Real or Junk. You are the filter now.' Name the controls and offer a tap alternative to dragging. hi and te already avoid colour.

flags.quote: Girls are bad at maths, so the homework is easy this week
flags.problem: A gender stereotype about ability, used as a sample 'real' message. hi/te use 'Maths homework is on page 42'. The English bh.i2 ('homework reminder') also refers to a message that does not exist in this wording.
flags.why: Breaks fairness-representation (India checklist: girls bad at maths or technology is always blocking).
flags.fix: Replace with 'Maths homework is on page 42' to match hi/te and bh.i2.

flags.quote: Messages from people with Muslim names are usually junk
flags.problem: Communal framing that labels a religious group as untrustworthy, shown to learners as a message to sort. Also, English bh.i6 says 'The football message' while hi/te use a cricket message and the symbol is 🏏.
flags.why: Breaks fairness-representation (India checklist: religious or communal framing of scams or danger is always blocking). Muslim learners could be directly harmed.
flags.fix: Replace with a neutral real message such as 'Cricket practice moved to Friday' (as in hi/te) and change bh.i6 to 'The cricket message'.

flags.quote: "weight": 3 (money); label knob.money: “Money words (2 points each)”
flags.problem: The money weight is 3 but the label in all three locales says 2 points. b6 uses weight 2, and the worked examples in b5 (3 + 4 + 3, 6 + 2 + 3, 2 money words = 4) all assume 2. With weight 3 the maximum score is 10 + 9 + 9 = 28, which exceeds the output max of 25. With weight 2 the maximum is exactly 25.
flags.why: Breaks numbers-and-working: the interactive gives different scores from the text and the compare block.
flags.fix: Set b4.config.model.inputs[1].weight to 2.

flags.quote: Score 10: exactly on the threshold. One more clue and it goes to junk; one fewer and it reaches the inbox.
flags.problem: The rule is 'score 10 or more goes to junk' (bh.rule), so a score of exactly 10 already goes to junk. 'One more clue and it goes to junk' is wrong. 'One fewer clue' may also mean a loss of 3 points, not 1. hi and te copy the same structure.
flags.why: Breaks numbers-and-working: the text contradicts the threshold rule.
flags.fix: Use: 'Score 10: exactly on the threshold, so it goes to junk. Take away 1 point and the score is 9, which reaches the inbox.' Apply the same to hi and te.

flags.quote: स्कोर 12: ठीक सीमा पर।
flags.problem: Hindi says score 12, but the goal, target and threshold are all 10. 12 is not 'exactly on the line'.
flags.why: Breaks locale-fidelity and numbers-and-working: the Hindi number differs from English and from the config goal target of 10.
flags.fix: Change to 'स्कोर 10: ठीक सीमा पर।' and apply the F08 correction.

flags.quote: "id": "i1", "value": 12 (text: 3 “!”, 2 money words, 1 urgent word (3 + 4 + 3))
flags.problem: 3 + 4 + 3 = 10, not 12. The stated working and the value disagree in every locale. At score 10 the item is still junk, but the displayed score is wrong. If F07 is not fixed, i5 (6 + 3 + 3 = 12) and i7 (2 × 3 = 6) would also break.
flags.why: Breaks numbers-and-working: every step of a calculation must add up.
flags.fix: Set b5.config.items[0].value to 10 (after setting the money weight to 2, items i3 = 3, i5 = 11 and i7 = 4 are correct).

flags.quote: Girls always write like the excited one.
flags.problem: Generalises a writing style to all girls. hi and te do not have this sentence.
flags.why: Breaks fairness-representation: attributing behaviour to a gender is blocking.
flags.fix: Delete the sentence so English matches hi/te: 'Two versions of the same real message from a friend.'

flags.quote: Village students usually fail it, but the idea is the same
flags.problem: Says rural students usually fail exams. hi and te do not contain it.
flags.why: Breaks fairness-representation: rural or poor people as the ignorant ones is always blocking.
flags.fix: Delete the sentence: 'Think of an exam with a pass mark. Each answer earns marks, the marks are added up, and if the total reaches the pass mark, you pass.'

flags.quote: This comparison works perfectly in every way, so you can think of the filter as an examiner.
flags.problem: States no break point, claims the analogy is perfect, and invites the learner to treat the filter as an examiner who understands answers. hi and te give a real break point (an examiner reads and understands, the filter only counts).
flags.why: Breaks analogy-integrity and Article 7. It also pushes the AI-has-a-mind misconception.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te meaning: 'Here the comparison stops working. An examiner reads and understands your answers. The filter only counts clues and has no idea what the message means.'

flags.quote: Real filters use exactly three clues, the same three as ours, and the points are always set by hand. That is what training means.
flags.problem: False on three counts: real filters use hundreds of clues, they are not the same three, and training is not setting points by hand. hi and te state it correctly.
flags.why: Breaks factual-accuracy: a simplification that becomes false. It teaches the misconception that someone wrote all the rules.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te meaning: 'Real filters use hundreds of clues. Nobody sets their points by hand: the filter works them out from millions of messages that people marked as junk. That is what training means.'

flags.quote: when a person types every rule into the program by hand
flags.problem: Defines training as the opposite of what it is. hi and te give the right definition (the program works out its own settings from many examples).
flags.why: Breaks factual-accuracy: a wrong glossary definition is learnt with every later use of the term.
flags.fix: Use: 'when a program works out its own settings from many examples, instead of a person setting them by hand'.

flags.quote: Choosing the threshold is easy: set it high enough and the filter never makes a mistake.
flags.problem: A high threshold lets more junk through. Every threshold trades one kind of mistake for another. 'Easy' is also a banned filler. hi and te state the trade-off correctly.
flags.why: Breaks factual-accuracy (the lesson then fails to teach the idea in ai-misconceptions #9).
flags.fix: Use the hi/te meaning: 'Choosing the threshold is a trade-off. A low threshold catches more junk but also stops more real messages. A high one lets real messages in, but more junk gets in too. No setting makes no mistakes.'

flags.quote: Wrong! Its score is 0, because it has no clues. Is 0 at least 10?
flags.problem: Opens feedback on a wrong choice with 'Wrong!'. hi and te omit it.
flags.why: Breaks respect-and-tone and Article 8: wrong answers meet curiosity, not judgement.
flags.fix: Use: 'Let us check the score. It has no clues, so its score is 0. Is 0 at least 10?'

flags.quote: so obviously the message goes to the inbox
flags.problem: Uses the banned filler 'obviously'. It does not demean the learner, but it tells the learner the step should be easy. hi and te omit it.
flags.why: Article 6 banned phrase; advisory because it does not demean.
flags.fix: Delete 'obviously': 'Score 0 is below the threshold of 10, so the message goes to the inbox.'

flags.quote: Send a few of these junk messages to your classmates’ phones and see if their filters catch them
flags.problem: Tells learners to send junk messages to other people's devices without their agreement. It also does not match br.r1 ('The filter no longer sees a money word'), which is about hiding a word. hi and te correctly change one letter of a word.
flags.why: Breaks safe-suggestions: sending tests to other people's devices is never allowed (learner-online-safety).
flags.fix: Use the hi/te idea: 'Write “FREE” with spaces, as “F R E E”'. This works inside the simulation and keeps r1 correct.

flags.quote: A real message lands in junk, next to the gambling and adult-content messages that fill it.
flags.problem: Refers to gambling and adult content in an aside for ages 13-17. hi and te do not contain it.
flags.why: Breaks age-appropriateness: no gambling or adult references, even in asides.
flags.fix: Delete the clause: 'Ten exclamation marks score 10 points. A real message lands in junk.'

flags.quote: Start each one with your full name, your school and your phone number, so the filter can learn about you.
flags.problem: Asks the learner to type name, school and phone number, and the classroom config (maxItems 12) suggests entries may be pooled. hi and te ask for messages to fool the filter instead and do not collect personal data.
flags.why: Breaks privacy and Article 10: v1 collects no personal data from children.
flags.fix: Use the hi/te prompt: 'Write up to five messages you think will fool this filter. Count the clues in each and work out its score from the points above: will it reach 10?'

flags.quote: so the filter can learn about you
flags.problem: Claims the filter learns about the learner, which is false for this filter and reinforces misconception #4.
flags.why: Breaks ai-framing: no claim that a system learns about or remembers the learner.
flags.fix: Remove it. The F21 fix removes the whole clause.

flags.quote: Write up to five messages ... (en), पाँच तक ऐसे संदेश लिखिए ... (hi), ... ఐదు వరకు రాయండి (te)
flags.problem: A free-text input in every locale never says that what is typed stays on this device. Example yd.e1 also models giving an address in a made-up scam message.
flags.why: Breaks privacy (learner-online-safety: inputs must say what you type stays on this device).
flags.fix: Add to each locale: 'What you type stays on this device. Use made-up messages only. Never type real names, numbers or addresses.'

flags.quote: A quick way to learn: click every prize link you get and see which ones are real. Each click adds to what you know, like runs in cricket.
flags.problem: Model answer tells learners to click every prize link. It is also not a threshold analogy and states no break point, while hi/te give a cricket 150-run model with a break point.
flags.why: Breaks safe-suggestions (never click unknown links, even to test) and analogy-integrity (every analogy states where it breaks).
flags.fix: Replace with the hi/te model answer: 'A cricket team needs 150 runs to win. Each run adds up and 150 is the line. But a team can watch the match and change its plan; the filter cannot see anything beyond the clues.'

flags.quote: It knows what junk is now, and it will remember me next time.
flags.problem: The takeaway says the filter knows and remembers the learner. The learner's filter has fixed weights and learns nothing. hi and te say it adds clues and never understands.
flags.why: Breaks ai-framing: the takeaway states the mind-framing and contradicts the lesson's own objective o2.
flags.fix: Use: 'I built a junk filter today. It adds up clues into a score and compares the score with a line. It never understands the message.'

flags.quote: Most students in your class got this one wrong.
flags.problem: An invented claim about what the learner's classmates did. The platform collects no such data. It also shames a learner who may have answered correctly. hi and te omit it.
flags.why: Breaks sourcing-and-honesty (no invented social proof), Article 11, and Article 8.
flags.fix: Delete it: 'The filter only counts clues, so an excited friend and a scammer can look alike to it.'

flags.quote: తెలివి లేని వాళ్ళే ఇలాంటి సందేశాలకు మోసపోతారు, మీరు అలా కాదు కదా?
flags.problem: The English hook question is 'So how did a program decide, about a message it had never seen before?'. The Telugu replaces it with 'Only unintelligent people get fooled by such messages, you are not like that, are you?', which insults learners and drops the lesson's puzzle.
flags.why: Breaks locale-fidelity, respect-and-tone and Article 8: judgemental language that implies victims are unintelligent, and the hook no longer sets up the lesson.
flags.fix: Translate the English question: 'అయితే ఒక ప్రోగ్రామ్, తాను ఇంతకు ముందు ఎప్పుడూ చూడని సందేశం గురించి ఎలా నిర్ణయించింది?'. Have a native speaker confirm.

flags.quote: मीटिंग 3 बजे हो गई है।
flags.problem: English is 'Meeting moved to 3 pm' (and Telugu says it moved). The Hindi 'हो गई है' means the meeting has already happened, which changes the meaning of the scenario.
flags.why: Breaks locale-fidelity: the Hindi does not keep the English meaning.
flags.fix: Use: 'मीटिंग 3 बजे के लिए बदल दी गई है।'
